source.title: Unified View of Grokking, Double Descent and Emergent Abilities: A Perspective from Circuits Competition
source.authors: Yu-Fei Huang; Sheng-Ding Hu; Xu Han; Zhi-Yuan Liu; Mao-Song Sun

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model hidden size and training-data quantity and measures validation performance on algorithmic tasks, conceptually testing double-descent and data-size claims with a different experimental setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own model-size and data-size sweeps. The parameter-norm comparison and memorization-capacity results are not rows for these claim versions. Values in Figures 6 and 7 are mainly described qualitatively rather than given as exact numerical validation accuracies.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps transformer hidden size at several training-set sizes and reports final validation accuracy, a direct model-wise double-descent test in a new setting: 1-layer transformers on modular arithmetic.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that model-wise double descent (seen as a rise-dip-rise in validation accuracy) arises when training data is well below the intersection of memorization capacity and critical dataset size. Models then pass through progression, ungrokking, semi-grokking and grokking. More data removes it, while harder tasks make it more prominent. They note the limitation to algorithmic tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies model hidden size and training-data quantity and measures validation performance, but uses its own modular algorithmic tasks and a 1-layer transformer setup rather than reproducing the original study's broader settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The size-wise curve changes with training-data quantity and task complexity: the reported double descent is weaker at 3000 modular-addition samples and absent at 4000 and 5000; a more complex task makes it more pronounced at 3000 samples.

fits_no_version.finding: The occurrence of model-wise double descent is predicted by where the training-set size sits relative to the intersection of memorization capacity (rising with size) and critical dataset size for grokking (falling with size). Raising task difficulty shifts that intersection and makes double descent more prominent at fixed data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-wise double descent in grokking-prone settings arises from memorization–generalization circuit competition and appears only when training data lies below the capacity/critical-dataset-size intersection.

record.problems: The experiments are limited to algorithmic tasks and a particular transformer setup; the authors note the need to extend to more realistic tasks and models. Several curve outcomes are described qualitatively, with exact values unavailable in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the listed versions were left out.

untested.parts: The study gives no explicit quantification that the peak coincides with the size that just fits the training set. The framework places the dip where the model can first memorize all data (ungrokking), but no row reports train accuracy at the dip.
Not tested. Training curves show grokking and semi-grokking plateaus, not a fall-rise-fall in test error over epochs.
Not tested near the interpolation threshold. The data-size sweep covers only regimes where models fully interpolate.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested.
No label-noise or regularization sweep; weight decay is fixed. No multiple-peak analysis.

missing.what: Train-accuracy curves alongside validation accuracy across hidden size. These would show whether the validation dip coincides with the onset of full training-set fitting (interpolation), which V1's peak location needs.
missing.locator: Figure 6 (a)-(d) train curves; Section 3 ungrokking definition

missing.what: Memorization capacity versus hidden size (random labels on all 12,769 pairs). This would give the size at which each training set can just be fit.

record.verdict_notes: All experiments use AdamW with weight decay, clean labels and 1-layer transformers on modular arithmetic. The dip is a collapse to zero validation accuracy from pure memorization (ungrokking), a mechanism distinct from the label-noise interpolation peak in the original sources. Values are read from figures and text, with no tables. The study is a preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests model-size trends on modular addition and a more complex modular task, but does not quantify how the peak aligns with the exact size at which the training set is just fit.
The paper discusses training-time grokking dynamics but does not test whether test error over epochs follows a fall-rise-fall double-descent curve.

The data-size trend is reported for modular addition, particularly for hidden size 64 near an approximate critical dataset size; the study does not establish a general effect across tasks or model classes.
Experiments use transformer models on algorithmic tasks, not a sweep across model classes.
The study proposes a circuits-competition account but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
The study does not test label-noise or regularization dependence of the peak, multiple descent peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that turns the curve into an ordinary U-shape.

rows.subject: 1-layer simplified decoder-only transformer (4 attention heads)
rows.operation_detail: Vary training dataset size and measure final validation accuracy
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy as training dataset size changes
rows.value: The text reports semi-grokking over training-data sizes 2000–3000 and generally improving generalization as training size approaches the approximate critical size of 3000; near-perfect validation accuracy is reported at 3000.
rows.note: In this reported near-critical range, adding data is associated with improved rather than worsened validation performance. Exact values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Not 'reversed'. The data sweep (2000–4000) is a grokking experiment where all models reach perfect training accuracy within a few epochs. Every point is past the data-axis interpolation threshold, so the near-threshold region V3 names is not sampled. The 'critical dataset size' (~3000) is a grokking threshold, not the interpolation threshold.
